title-group.article-title: The Effect of Efavirenz and Rufinamide on the Pharmacokinetics and Safety of Quizartinib: Two Phase 1 Studies in Healthy Participants

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Quizartinib is an oral, potent, selective FMS‐like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) inhibitor, approved for the treatment of FLT3‐internal tandem duplication (ITD)–positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and under investigation in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD–negative AML. Quizartinib is metabolized by cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) in vitro, primarily into the active metabolite AC886, a CYP3A substrate. These phase 1, open‐label, randomized, parallel‐group trials assessed the effect of efavirenz, a moderate CYP3A inducer, and rufinamide, a weak CYP3A inducer, on the pharmacokinetics of quizartinib and AC886, and the safety and tolerability of quizartinib in healthy participants. Each study enrolled 32 participants; 16 received 60 mg quizartinib alone and 16 received 60 mg quizartinib plus either 600 mg efavirenz or 400 mg rufinamide. Coadministration with efavirenz decreased the maximum plasma concentration (C max) and area under the plasma concentration–time curve extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) of quizartinib by ~45% and ~90%, respectively, versus quizartinib alone; AC886 C max and AUCinf also decreased by ~68% and ~96%, respectively. Coadministration with rufinamide had modest impact on quizartinib exposure (C max and AUCinf decreased by ~19% and ~34%, respectively, vs. quizartinib alone). Coadministration of rufinamide and quizartinib decreased AC886 C max and AUCinf by ~47% and ~53%, respectively, versus quizartinib alone. Quizartinib was well tolerated and no new safety signals were observed. These results suggest that concomitant use of quizartinib and moderate CYP3A inducers should be avoided. Concomitant use of weak CYP3A inducers does not warrant dose adjustment, since the impact on quizartinib exposure is clinically nonrelevant.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Quizartinib is an oral, potent, selective, FMS‐like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) inhibitor approved for the treatment of FLT3‐internal tandem duplication (ITD)–positive AML. Quizartinib is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A), and its exposure is increased by strong CYP3A inhibitors like ketoconazole.

What question did this study address? ○
These two phase 1 drug–drug interaction trials assessed the pharmacokinetics of quizartinib and its active metabolite, AC886, when coadministered with either efavirenz or rufinamide, a moderate and a weak CYP3A inducer, respectively, to inform dosing recommendations when quizartinib is used concomitantly with CYP3A inducers.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
Coadministration of quizartinib with efavirenz decreased exposure of both quizartinib and AC886, compared with quizartinib alone. The impact of rufinamide on quizartinib and AC886 exposure was modest but not clinically relevant.

How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○
The outcomes of these studies indicate that concomitant use of quizartinib and moderate CYP3A inducers, including efavirenz, is recommended to be avoided. The use of quizartinib with weak CYP3A inducers does not warrant dose adjustment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Quizartinib is an oral, selective, second‐generation, type II FMS‐like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) inhibitor with potent binding affinity against wild‐type FLT3, FLT3‐internal tandem duplication (ITD), and several FLT3 variants with point mutations within the kinase domain [1, 2, 3, 4]. Quizartinib is currently approved for the treatment of patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) FLT3‐ITD–positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in Japan, based on the outcomes of the QuANTUM‐R phase 3 trial (NCT02039726), in which quizartinib improved the overall survival (OS) in patients with R/R FLT3‐ITD–positive AML compared with salvage chemotherapy (median 6.2 vs. 4.7 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.76, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.58–0.98; p = 0.02) [5]. Quizartinib is also approved for use in adults with newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD–positive AML worldwide, based on the results of the QuANTUM‐First Phase 3 trial (NCT02668653), in which quizartinib in combination with induction and consolidation chemotherapy, followed by maintenance therapy with quizartinib alone significantly improved OS in adults with FLT3‐ITD–positive AML compared with placebo (median 31.9 vs. 15.1 months; HR, 0.78, 95% CI, 0.62–0.98; p = 0.032) [6].

Quizartinib has also been assessed in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD–negative AML in the phase 2 QUIWI trial (NCT04107727), where median OS was significantly prolonged with quizartinib versus placebo (not reached vs. 29.3 months, respectively; HR, 0.63, 95% CI, 0.44–0.91; p = 0.012) [7], and is currently under investigation in the phase 3 QuANTUM‐Wild trial (NCT06578247) in adults with newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD–negative AML [8].

Following oral administration under fasted conditions, quizartinib is rapidly absorbed, with median time to peak concentration (T max) being approximately 4 h (range 2–8 h), and it is extensively metabolized by the cytochrome P450 (CYP)3A with a mean (standard deviation [SD]) effective half‐life (t 1/2) in patients with newly diagnosed AML of 81 h (±73) [9]. AC886 is identified as the major active circulating mono‐oxidative metabolite constituting approximately 58% of the parent exposure [10] and with a mean (SD) t 1/2 of 136 h (±113) [9]. In vitro, quizartinib is primarily metabolized via oxidation by CYP3A4/5, and AC886 is formed and metabolized by CYP3A4/5 [9].

Quizartinib drug–drug interaction (DDI) potential has been assessed in a clinical study with CYP3A inhibitors. In healthy adults, coadministration of quizartinib (single dose of 30 mg) with the strong CYP3A inhibitor ketoconazole increased quizartinib maximum plasma concentration (C max) and area under the plasma concentration–time curve extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) by 17% and 94%, respectively, compared with quizartinib alone; coadministration with the moderate CYP3A inhibitor fluconazole increased quizartinib C max and AUCinf by 11% and 20%, respectively. Concomitant use of ketoconazole decreased AC886 C max and AUCinf by 60% and 15%, respectively, whereas coadministration with fluconazole resulted in minimal changes to AC886 exposure compared with quizartinib alone [11]. These findings led to recommendations for adjustments of the quizartinib dose when coadministered with strong CYP3A inhibitors: specifically, the quizartinib dose should be reduced to 30 mg/day in patients receiving 60 mg/day, and to 20 mg/day in patients receiving 40 or 30 mg/day; no dose adjustment is required during concomitant use of quizartinib and a moderate CYP3A inhibitor [9].

To inform potential quizartinib dose adjustments when used concomitantly with moderate and weak CYP3A inducers, two phase 1 clinical studies were conducted. These studies investigated the effect of coadministration with efavirenz, a moderate CYP3A inducer, and rufinamide, a weak CYP3A inducer, on the pharmacokinetics (PK) and safety of quizartinib.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: The AC220‐A‐U106 (“U106”; NCT04459598) and AC220‐164 (“164”; NCT06740825) studies were Phase 1, open‐label, randomized, parallel‐group, single‐center trials in healthy participants evaluating the impact of CYP3A induction on the plasma PK, safety, and tolerability of quizartinib and plasma PK of AC886. The U106 study assessed concomitant use of quizartinib with the moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz, and was conducted at Worldwide Clinical Trials, San Antonio, Texas, United States, between August and November 2020. The 164 study assessed the coadministration of quizartinib with the weak CYP3A inducer rufinamide and was conducted at the same clinical research unit (CRU) between October and December 2024.

Both clinical trials followed the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Council for Harmonization Guideline E6 for Good Clinical Practice, and local regulatory requirements. The protocols of the studies U106 and 164, any amendments, and all other relevant study documents were reviewed and approved by IntegReview Institutional Review Board (protocol number 5011003; August 12, 2020) and Advarra Institutional Review Board (approval number MOD02376662; January 22, 2025), respectively. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to screening.

sec.title: Study Participants
sec.p: Both studies used the same inclusion criteria. Eligible participants were 18–55 years of age, with a body mass index of 18–32 kg/m2. Alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and total bilirubin levels were required to be equal or below the upper limit of normal, and hemoglobin equal or above the lower limit of normal (≥ 11.5 g/dL for females and ≥ 12.5 g/dL for males). Resting heart rate was required to be 50–100 beats per minute, systolic blood pressure 90–145 mmHg, and diastolic blood pressure 50–95 mmHg. Participants agreed to refrain from consuming fruits known to affect CYP3A (e.g., grapefruits).

Candidates with any clinically significant disease, including cardiovascular, respiratory, hematologic, gastrointestinal, central nervous system disorders, hepatic/renal impairment, thyroid dysfunction, pituitary malfunction, adrenal insufficiency, history of allergy or hypersensitivity, alcohol or drug dependence, or a positive test for infections such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or hepatitis, were excluded from the studies. Use or planned use of medications known to inhibit or induce CYP3A (including supplements containing St. John's Wort) other than the study drugs from 14 days or 5 half‐lives (whichever was longer) prior to quizartinib administration was also prohibited.
All inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in the supplement of this manuscript.

sec.title: Treatment and Assessments of the AC220‐A‐U106 Study
sec.p: Participants of the U106 study were admitted to the CRU on the day prior to randomization and dosing (Day −1). Group A received oral efavirenz 600 mg on an empty stomach on Day 1 and continued the regimen through Day 35, as well as a single oral dose of 60 mg quizartinib (2 × 30 mg) under fasting conditions on Day 15 only. Blood samples for PK analyses were collected on Days 15–36 and safety assessments were conducted on Days 1–36. Check‐out was performed on Day 36. Group B received a single oral dose of 60 mg quizartinib (2 × 30 mg) on Day 1 under fasting conditions. Blood samples were collected and safety assessments were conducted on Days 1–22. Check‐out was performed on Day 22. Safety monitoring was carried out for an additional 30 days after completion of study treatment in both groups (Figure 1).

sec.title: Treatment and Assessments of the AC220‐164 Study
sec.p: Participants of the 164 study were admitted to the CRU and randomized on the day prior to dosing (Day −1). Group A received 400 mg of oral rufinamide twice daily (BID) on Days 1–32, and a single oral dose of quizartinib 60 mg (2 × 30 mg) on Day 12, together with standard meals. Blood samples were collected on Days 12–33 and safety assessments were conducted on Days 1–33. Check‐out was done on Day 33, and participants returned to the CRU for a safety follow‐up visit on Day 40. Group B received a single oral dose of quizartinib 60 mg (2 × 30 mg) on Day 1, with a standard meal. Blood sampling and safety assessments were carried out on Days 1–22. Checkout was performed on Day 22 and no additional safety follow‐up visits were required for Group B (Figure 1).

sec.title: Dose Selection
sec.p: Quizartinib 60 mg/day was selected as the study dose, consistent with the dosing regimen evaluated in the pivotal QUANTUM‐First study [6]. The efavirenz dose of 600 mg/day reflects the approved dose in the United States for the treatment of HIV infection and has been evaluated in previous clinical studies [12]. The rufinamide dose of 400 mg BID was based on previous DDI studies in healthy volunteers [13] and corresponds to the approved dose in the United States for the adjunctive treatment of seizures associated with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome in adults.

In U106, quizartinib was administered orally in the morning with approximately 240 mL of water following a 10‐h overnight fast; participants remained fasted for 4 h post‐dose. Efavirenz was administered orally before bedtime on an empty stomach, with fasting required for at least 2 h before and after dosing. In 164, quizartinib was administered orally in the morning with a standard meal (concomitantly with rufinamide in Group A), and rufinamide was administered BID with standard meals (breakfast/dinner), with doses separated by at least 8 h.

sec.title: PK Analyses
sec.p: The PK endpoints of the two studies included C max, AUC up to the last quantifiable timepoint (AUClast), and AUCinf of quizartinib and AC886. Additionally, T max and t 1/2 were assessed for quizartinib and AC886; oral clearance (CL/F) and apparent volume of distribution during the terminal phase (Vz/F) were assessed for quizartinib only. Metabolite‐to‐parent ratios (MPRs) were calculated for AUClast and AUCinf. Blood samples were collected pre‐dose and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, 144, 216, 288, 360, 432, and 504 h post‐quizartinib dose for U106, and pre‐dose and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, 144, 192, 240, 288, 336, 384, 432, 480, and 504 h post‐quizartinib dose for 164.

Quizartinib and AC886 plasma concentrations were measured using a validated liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry method by BASi (Bioanalytical Systems Inc., West Lafayette, IN, USA) as previously reported, with an analytical range of 0.500–500 ng/mL for both analytes [11, 14].

Plasma quizartinib and AC886 concentration–time data acquired during bioanalysis were analyzed via noncompartmental analysis methods using Phoenix WinNonlin (Version 8.3.4, Certara, USA Inc.) in conjunction with Certara Integral (Version 24.4.3, Certara, USA Inc.). In the PK analysis, concentration values below the limit of quantification (BLQ) at the beginning of the PK profile up to the first quantifiable concentration were set to zero; missing and terminal BLQ values were set to missing. Quantifiable data points followed by two or more consecutive BLQ values were set to missing. Actual sampling times relative to dosing were used in all analyses.

sec.title: Safety Assessments
sec.p: Secondary endpoints included treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs), vital signs, 12‐lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), clinical laboratory tests (chemistry and hematology), and physical examinations. Adverse events were coded using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA 23.0 and 27.1). TEAEs were summarized and graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. The number and percentage of participants reporting treatment‐emergent and treatment‐related serious adverse events (SAEs) were tabulated, as were TEAEs of special interest (AESIs) and TEAEs leading to discontinuation of study drug. Vital signs and ECG were assessed on Day −1 (164 only), pre‐dose, Day 1, Day 2 (164 only), Day 4 (164 only), and at Day 22 relative to quizartinib administration.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: The PK analysis comprised all participants who were dosed and had sufficient data to calculate at least one planned PK parameter; the safety analysis set included all randomized participants who received at least one dose of the study drug. C max, AUClast, and AUCinf were compared between Group A (quizartinib plus either efavirenz or rufinamide, “Test”) and Group B (quizartinib alone, “Reference”). Between‐group comparisons were performed using an ANOVA model and based on logarithm‐transformed C max, AUClast, and AUCinf. Least square means of differences between groups, and 90% CIs were exponentiated to get the geometric mean ratio (Test/Reference) and corresponding 90% CI of the ratio on the untransformed scale. PK summary statistics and ANOVAs were generated with and without participants with AUCinf extrapolated > 20%. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS (Version 9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

sec.title: Demographic and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: A total of 32 healthy adults were enrolled in each study. In U106, all participants were included in the safety population, and 31 were included in the PK analysis set (Figure S1); in the 164 study, all randomized participants were included in both the PK and safety populations (Figure S2). Across both studies, mean group age ranged from 36.5–40.5 years, most participants were male, and mean body mass index ranged from 26.3–27.7 kg/m2. Demographics and baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: PK Analyses
sec.p: Mean plasma concentration–time profiles for quizartinib and AC886, with and without coadministration of efavirenz, are shown in Figure 2 and Figure S3. Following oral administration of quizartinib, peak quizartinib concentrations occurred at approximately 2–4 h post‐dose in both groups (Table 2). Maximum quizartinib exposure (C max) was reduced by ~45% and total quizartinib exposures (AUClast and AUCinf) were reduced by about 89%–90% after coadministration with efavirenz compared with administration of quizartinib alone (Table 3). Terminal t 1/2 was shorter after concurrent administration of quizartinib with efavirenz (23.8 ± 7.4 h [mean ± SD, hereafter]) than quizartinib alone (136 ± 40.1 h). Quizartinib CL/F was higher and Vz/F was larger after coadministration with efavirenz versus quizartinib alone (12.2 ± 7.69 L/h vs. 1.19 ± 0.532 L/h and 360 ± 102 L vs. 211 ± 60.0 L, respectively [mean ± SD]) (Table 2).

sec.p: For AC886, peak concentrations were observed at around 4.0 h post‐dose in both groups (Table 2). Coadministration with efavirenz reduced AC886 C max by ~68%, and AUClast and AUCinf by ~96% each compared with quizartinib alone (Table 3). AC886 t 1/2 was substantially shorter with efavirenz (11.9 ± 5.5 h) than without efavirenz (135 ± 33.5 h) (Table 2). MPR values for AUClast and AUCinf were reduced by approximately 64% and 59%, respectively, after coadministration of quizartinib and efavirenz versus quizartinib alone.

Mean plasma concentration–time profiles for quizartinib and AC886, with and without coadministration of rufinamide, are shown in Figure 3 and Figure S4. Quizartinib T max ranged between 4.0–8.0 h regardless of coadministration with rufinamide (Table 2). Compared with quizartinib alone, coadministration of rufinamide reduced quizartinib C max, AUClast, and AUCinf by approximately 19%, 31%, and 34%, respectively (Table 3). Quizartinib t 1/2 was slightly shorter after coadministration of quizartinib and rufinamide (101 ± 20.1 h) than that of quizartinib alone (133 ± 27.2 h). Coadministration with rufinamide increased quizartinib CL/F compared with quizartinib alone (4.04 ± 1.31 L/h vs. 2.63 ± 0.673 L/h, respectively). Additionally, quizartinib Vz/F was larger after combination therapy (577 ± 202 L) than with quizartinib alone (494 ± 119 L) (Table 2).

caption.p: Concentration–time profiles of (A) quizartinib (left: Semi‐log scale; right: Linear in the first 48 h) and (B) AC886 in study AC220‐164 (left: Semi‐log scale; right: Linear in the first 48 h). Data are shown as means ± standard deviations. h, hour(s).

sec.p: For AC886 median T max (range) was 8.0 h (6.0–48.1) with concomitant rufinamide and 24.0 h (4.0–48.0 h) after quizartinib alone (Table 2). Coadministration with rufinamide reduced AC886 C max, AUClast, and AUCinf by approximately 47%, 48%, and 53%, respectively, compared with administration of quizartinib alone (Table 3). AC886 t 1/2 was slightly shorter after coadministration of quizartinib and rufinamide (115 ± 25.8 h) compared with administration of quizartinib alone (132 ± 33.2 h). Mean MPR values for AUClast and AUCinf were approximately 25% and 28% lower, respectively, after the co‐administration of quizartinib and rufinamide than with those after administration of quizartinib alone (Table 2).

sec.title: Safety Assessment
sec.p: Across both studies, TEAEs were generally mild (Table S1). In the U106 study, TEAEs were reported by 18/32 (56.3%) participants: 13/16 (81.3%) in Group A (quizartinib plus efavirenz) and 5/16 (31.3%) in Group B (quizartinib alone) (Table S2). In the 164 study, TEAEs occurred in 11/32 (34.4%) participants: 6/16 (37.5%) in Group A (quizartinib plus rufinamide) and 5/16 (31.3%) in Group B (quizartinib alone) (Table S3). No Grade ≥ 2 TEAEs were reported in either study. In U106, the most commonly reported TEAEs related to the study medication were dizziness (25.0%), nausea (18.8%), and flatulence (18.8%) in Group A and nausea (6.3%) and headache (6.3%) in Group B. No TEAEs were considered treatment‐related during the 164 study. There were no deaths, SAEs, or AESI in any participant in either study. There were no clinically significant laboratory abnormalities or changes in vital signs reported in any participant during both studies. Two participants of U106, one with arthropod bite and cellulitis in Group A, and one with syphilis in Group B, had early terminations due to TEAEs, which were considered not treatment‐related. Overall, there were no clinically significant findings for ECG data: during U106, one (6.3%) participant in Group A and three (18.8%) in Group B had an increase in the QT interval of > 60 ms from baseline; in 164, one participant in Group B had an increased QT interval of > 60 ms from baseline and one participant in Group B had a QT interval corrected using Fridericia's method (QTcF) interval of > 450 ms. No participant in either study had QTcF values > 480 ms (Table S4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Quizartinib and its active metabolite, AC886, are substrates of CYP3A, and their PK can be affected by concomitant use of drugs that are CYP3A modulators. Therefore, investigation of the use of quizartinib with CYP3A modulators is necessary to inform dosing guidance for patients receiving quizartinib in clinical settings.

Quizartinib exposure is affected by concomitant use of strong CYP3A inhibitors (such as ketoconazole), whereas the effect of coadministration of quizartinib with a moderate CYP3A inhibitor (fluconazole) on quizartinib exposure is minimal and clinically nonrelevant [11]. Here, we report that concurrent administration of efavirenz (a moderate CYP3A4 inducer) markedly reduced the exposure of quizartinib and AC886 (U106 study), while coadministration of rufinamide (a weak CYP3A4 inducer) led to a modest reduction in quizartinib and AC886 exposure (164 study). Coadministration with efavirenz reduced quizartinib C max by ~45% and AC886 C max by ~68%, and reduced quizartinib AUClast and AUCinf by approximately 89%–90% and AC886 AUClast and AUCinf by ~96% each, versus quizartinib alone. The greater extent of decreases in AUClast and AUCinf compared with the C max decreases indicates greater increases in systemic elimination versus pre‐systemic metabolism, further supported by a shortened t ½. MPR values based on AUClast and AUCinf were reduced by approximately 59% to 64% after coadministration of quizartinib and efavirenz compared with quizartinib alone. This decrease due to the concomitant use of quizartinib with a CYP3A inducer confirms that AC886 is also a substrate of CYP3A. Efavirenz is expected to reduce the exposure of CYP3A sensitive index substrates by 50% to 80% [15, 16]; however, the greater than expected 90% reduction in quizartinib AUClast and AUCinf when coadministered with efavirenz indicates the possible involvement of other mechanisms other than induction, including metabolic activation through conformational change of the CYP3A enzyme by efavirenz [15]. Coadministration of quizartinib and rufinamide reduced the C max of quizartinib and AC886 by approximately 19% and 47%, respectively, relative to administration of quizartinib alone, while AUCinf values were reduced by approximately 34% and 53%, respectively. This observed decrease in exposure of both quizartinib and AC886 is within the range of expected weak CYP3A induction of 20%–50% decrease in exposure and is considered not clinically significant, due to quizartinib's wide therapeutic window. A previous exposure–OS analysis of quizartinib in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3‐ITD–positive AML enrolled in the pivotal Phase 3 study QuANTUM‐First demonstrated a survival benefit across a wide range of quizartinib exposure [17]. After a ~35% reduction, similar to the reduction observed after coadministration of quizartinib with rufinamide, quizartinib exposure remains well within the efficacious range. Furthermore, in clinical practice, patients are not typically exposed to weak CYP3A inducers like rufinamide for extended periods of time. In addition, a previously reported population PK model of quizartinib in the same population of patients did not identify coadministration of a weak CYP3A inducer as a significant covariate warranting dose adjustments [18]. The magnitude of PK reduction observed in the 164 study, where participants received rufinamide 400 mg BID for 32 days, represents an extreme estimate. In clinical practice, a shorter duration of administration of CYP3A inducers is expected than the exposure to rufinamide of the volunteers of the 164 study.

The observed reductions in exposure with CYP3A inducers were directionally complementary to the increases observed with CYP3A inhibitors, collectively confirming CYP3A4 as the primary clearance pathway for quizartinib, though inducers demonstrated proportionally greater effects than inhibitors. Median quizartinib T max was comparable between the groups receiving concomitant rufinamide and those receiving quizartinib alone. In contrast, peak exposure of AC886 was observed at a median T max of 8 h after coadministration of quizartinib and rufinamide, ie, three‐fold earlier compared with administration of quizartinib alone (median T max, 24 h). This difference can be explained due to the flat PK profile of AC886 around the peak exposure resulting in a wide range of T max around the median. For both quizartinib and AC886, a slightly shorter t 1/2 was observed after coadministration of quizartinib and rufinamide than with t 1/2 after administration of quizartinib alone, which can be explained by the increased clearance due to CYP3A induction by rufinamide.

Overall, there were no new safety signals identified with quizartinib alone or when coadministered with CYP3A inducers during the studies, with the safety profile being consistent with known data from Phase 2 and 3 trials in adults with AML [5, 6, 19]. Treatment‐related TEAEs were numerically higher with the combination of efavirenz with quizartinib versus quizartinib alone; however, all events were Grade 1. In the 164 study, all observed TEAEs were Grade 1, and none were treatment‐related. No deaths, SAEs, or treatment‐related discontinuations were reported in both studies. There were no remarkable changes in laboratory parameters or vital signs. Close ECG monitoring was warranted given the known QT/QTcF‐prolongation liability of quizartinib and the potential for additive effects when coadministered with QT‐prolonging agents, including certain CYP3A inducers [9]. Several weak CYP3A inducers were considered for the DDI study and many factors contributed to the selection of rufinamide as the study drug. A particularly interesting characteristic of rufinamide is its known QT shortening effect (mean ≈20 ms at doses > 2400 mg BID) [20], which could potentially counteract and attenuate quizartinib‐induced QT prolongation. For these reasons, ECGs were collected more frequently during the 164 study. Across the two studies, coadministration with the moderate or weak CYP3A inducer resulted in only minor increases in QT and QTcF, consistent with the known effect of quizartinib. In the 164 study, the mean QTcF change from baseline to Day 12 of coadministration of quizartinib with rufinamide was minimal, confirming the opposing QT‐shortening effect of rufinamide.

In these studies, participants received a single 60 mg oral dose of quizartinib, which does not represent the prescribed dosing regimen for the induction or consolidation phases of quizartinib in patients with AML [9]. However, the relevance of this finding is maintained as the single‐dose 60 mg exposure matches the systemic exposure achieved at the steady‐state concentrations of lower, clinically relevant doses, thereby providing an appropriate assessment of the effect of the CYP3A induction on quizartinib PK. Moreover, given the linearity of quizartinib PK, extrapolation of the results to higher doses was possible.

The two study protocols differ in the conditions of administration of the drugs: in the U106 study, quizartinib and efavirenz were administered under fasting, whereas in the 164 study, participants received quizartinib and rufinamide with a standard meal. Quizartinib may be administered with or without food, and a prior food‐effect study has demonstrated no meaningful impact of food on its PK, with low interindividual variability [21]. In addition, rufinamide must be taken with food; therefore, the fed condition was required for the 164 study. Given the minimal and clinically nonrelevant effect of food on quizartinib exposure, this difference does not meaningfully impact the interpretation of the DDI results.

These two DDI studies demonstrated a substantial decrease in quizartinib systemic exposure after coadministration with efavirenz, a moderate CYP3A inducer (U106 study), while coadministration of rufinamide, a weak CYP3A inducer, led to a modest reduction in quizartinib exposure (164 study). As the reduced exposure of quizartinib may lead to reduced clinical benefit, concomitant use of quizartinib and moderate CYP3A inducers is recommended to be avoided. Similarly, strong CYP3A inducers are also expected to substantially decrease quizartinib exposure, which may reduce quizartinib efficacy. Thus, concomitant use of quizartinib and strong CYP3A inducers should also be avoided. The use of quizartinib with weak CYP3A inducers does not warrant dose adjustment, since the consequent decrease in quizartinib exposure is clinically nonrelevant.
